summaries.summary: Many automated stance detection datasets contain short texts about politicians or public issues annotated for stance toward a target, but are limited in scope.
Current stance detection methods face questionable cross-lingual performance, small single-target multilingual datasets, target-specific models, and lower cross-target performance.
The paper proposes x-stance, a larger dataset with more than 150 Swiss politics questions and more than 67k candidate answers from the last decade.
Questions are available in English, Swiss Standard German, French, and Italian, with comment language depending on the candidate's region of origin.
Data were extracted from Smartvote, where candidates give categorical answers and may add free-text comments justifying, explaining, or differentiating them.
The dataset becomes a stance detection task by treating the question as the target representation and the commentary as the input to classify.
The dataset is split for zero-shot cross-lingual and cross-target transfer, and a fine-tuned multilingual Bert baseline shows comparable accuracy and some generalization.
The dataset and code for reproducing the baseline model are publicly available.
IberEval produced two multilingual datasets of annotated Spanish and Catalan tweets focused on Catalan independence, described as the first truly multilingual stance detection datasets.

For x-stance languages, only monolingual datasets seem available: French presidential candidate tweets, Italian 2016 constitutional referendum tweets, and a German GermEval 2017 aspect-based sentiment dataset.
SemEval-2016 offered multiple targets, with target-specific models in subtask A and lower-performing cross-target transfer to “Donald Trump” in subtask B.
BIBREF4 introduced a multi-target stance dataset with two targets per instance, focusing on dependencies within a text sample rather than many samples with many targets.
In a target-specific setting, BIBREF10 systematically evaluated stance detection approaches and found Bert consistently outperformed previous approaches.
BIBREF10 used single-segment encoding preventing cross-target transfer, while BIBREF11 used conditional encoding with a bidirectional LSTM to generalize to unseen targets.
x-stance input consists of a natural language question about a political issue and a natural language commentary on a stance toward it.
The predicted label is `favor' or `against`, with no `neither' class, making x-stance a binary classification task.
The evaluation metric is the macro-average of the F1-score for `favor' and the F1-score for `against', used for comparability with previous benchmarks.
Questions and answers were downloaded via the Smartvote API, covering 175 communal, cantonal and national elections between 2011 and 2020.
Smartvote candidates answer the same translated questions with `yes', `rather yes', `rather no', or `no', and may add comments of at most 500 characters.
Smartvote questions were edited by political scientists to cover broad political issues relevant at election time, with design documentation provided by BIBREF12.
The two labels on each pole were merged into `favor' or `against' to improve consistency and comparability with previous stance detection datasets.
The text of the comments was not further preprocessed.
Because the API lacks comment language, langdetect BIBREF13 jointly classified all comments per responder, assuming no code-switching.
A first run allowed all 55 supported languages plus Romansh, finding no Romansh comments, unexpected outputs as misclassifications, and little or no Swiss German.
The second run restricted the identifier's output to English, French, German and Italian.
Questions and answers were pre-filtered for quality, with a focus on national-level questions and inclusion of all national election questions and answers.
For communal and cantonal elections, only answers to questions also asked nationally were used, augmenting training while validation and test sets used national election answers.
The less than 20 comments classified as English were discarded, and instances meeting listed conditions were filtered from the dataset.
Instances were filtered if the question is not closed or does not address a clearly defined political issue.
Instances were filtered if no comment was submitted or the comment is shorter than 50 characters.
Instances were filtered if the comment starts with “but” or a similar indicator that it is not self-contained.
Instances were filtered if the comment contains a URL.
In total, a fifth of the original comments were filtered out.
Smartvote editors organized questions into categories such as “Economy”, which were consolidated into 12 broad topics in Table TABREF7.
The dataset is shared under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license, with copyright remaining with www.smartvote.ch.
Respondent IDs are hashed, no personal attributes such as party affiliation are included, and a data statement BIBREF15 is provided in Appendix SECREF8.
“Healthcare” and “Political System” were held out from training to create a separate cross-topic test set with related questions and answers.
To test cross-question generalization within seen topics, 16 held-out questions were manually selected across the remaining 10 topics to ensure no paraphrases appeared in training.
Italian was designated test-only, while percentages of German and French respondents were randomly selected for validation or test respondents.
The split yielded one training set, one validation set and four test sets, with sizes in Table TABREF8 and no simultaneous cross-lingual and cross-target test sets.
Some observations can be made about the composition of x-stance.
Figure FIGREF23 shows `favor' and `against` proportions by target, with held-out topics at 49.4% `favor' and other topics at 50.0%.
Some questions are paraphrases of the same political issue, but duplicates are not consolidated because they contribute to training data diversity.
Some questions in the dataset are short, while others are rather convoluted, with a typical long question following.
A long question asks whether the 1% share of direct payments to Swiss agriculture going to organic farming should increase under Switzerland's 2014-2017 agricultural policy.
Such longer questions might be more challenging to process semantically.
x-stance has more German than French samples, with a language ratio of about 3:1 across all training and test sets, motivating a multi-source M-Bert baseline.
Two types of baselines are evaluated to obtain an impression of the task's difficulty.
Majority class baselines predict the most frequent class globally or target-wise, with the latter applicable only to the supervised test set.
Multilingual Bert (M-Bert), pretrained jointly in 104 languages, is fine-tuned as a baseline and has shown strong multilingual and stance detection performance.
The x-stance task is treated as sequence pair classification, with the question as segment A, the comment as segment B, [SEP], [CLS], and a linear layer.
The full model is fine-tuned with cross-entropy loss using the AllenNLP library BIBREF21 as the implementation basis.
The `favor' class was upsampled for balance, with a maximum sequence length of 512 subwords, batch size of 16, and grid search based on validation accuracy.
The grid search learning rates were 5e-5, 3e-5, and 2e-5.
The grid search numbers of epochs were 3 and 4.

Grid search was repeated independently for every variant, using Adam with ${\beta }_1=0.9$ and ${\beta }_2=0.999$, L2 weight decay of $0.01$, warmup over the first 10%, linear decay, and dropout probability of 0.1.
Table TABREF36 shows M-Bert consistently outperforms majority class baselines cross-lingually, including zero-short Italian performance above the target-wise majority class baseline.
Table TABREF37 shows M-Bert performs worse cross-target but surpasses majority class baselines, with cross-question score slightly lower than cross-topic score.
The default setup preserves horizontal language consistency by matching question and comment languages, including Italian questions for Italian test instances.
Vertical language consistency is tested by training and evaluating M-Bert with all questions in English, chosen as a lingua franca with the largest M-Bert pretraining share.
Table TABREF39 shows negligible effects in most settings but clearly increased cross-lingual performance when all questions are in English.
Additional experiments test whether only questions or only comments are necessary to optimally solve the task.
One experiment uses a single segment containing the comment and removes questions from training and test data (missing questions).
One experiment uses only the question and removes the comment (missing comments).
Both cases decrease performance across all evaluation settings, with much higher loss for missing comments, indicating comments contain the most important stance information.

Missing questions also reduce performance, especially in supervised and cross-lingual settings, while Table TABREF48 shows comments occurring with multiple targets and less pronounced effects in cross-target settings.
Single-segment experiments show both comment and question provide crucial information, and randomized test data probe whether M-Bert mainly uses one segment.
One probe keeps comments in place and randomly shuffles questions within the same test set and language (random questions).
One probe keeps questions in place and randomizes comments within test set boundaries (random comments).
Table TABREF39 shows performance decreases in both randomized cases, confirming the model learns to take into account both segments.
The final experiment tests whether targets need natural language representation or can instead use trainable embeddings.
Each target type is represented by a different reserved symbol from the M-Bert vocabulary, with segment A set to that symbol instead of a natural language question.

Table TABREF39 shows M-Bert with target embeddings performs clearly worse in supervised and cross-lingual settings, indicating spelled-out natural language questions provide important linguistic detail.
Baseline experiments confirm that M-Bert can achieve reasonable accuracy on x-stance.
Table TABREF46 lists Bert variant scores on other stance detection datasets, suggesting supervised x-stance has similar difficulty to SemEval-2016 BIBREF0 or MPCHI BIBREF22.
In cross-lingual and cross-target settings, the mean score drops by 6–8 percentage points compared to supervised, showing zero-shot transfer is possible but improvable.
Additional experiments in Table TABREF39 validate the results and justify the sequence-pair classification approach to stance detection.
Table TABREF47 shows high-confidence M-Bert errors, indicating many comments express stance implicitly, a potential dataset weakness partly compensated by the dataset's size and breadth.
The x-stance dataset covers broad national Swiss politics topics, enabling multi-target learning and multilingual stance detection in Swiss Standard German, French and Italian.
Formal commentary by politicians on political questions adds a new text genre, and a question–answer format naturally conditions stance detection models on a target.
Baseline results with multilingual Bert show some zero-shot transfer to unseen languages and targets, with a performance gap and potential value for other fields.
This work was funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation (project MUTAMUR; no. 176727), and Isabelle Augenstein is thanked for helpful feedback.
